passages.t: A decree that cannot be revoked
passages.happening:
‘That same day King Xerxes awarded Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews’ (verse 1). Esther tells the king how Mordecai is related to her, and the king gives Mordecai the signet ring he had taken back from Haman. Esther puts Mordecai over Haman's estate (verse 2).

But the decree still stands. ‘And once again, Esther addressed the king. She fell at his feet weeping and begged him to revoke the evil scheme of Haman the Agagite, which he had devised against the Jews’ (verse 3). The king holds out the gold scepter again. “For how could I bear to see the disaster that would befall my people? How could I bear to see the destruction of my kindred?” (verse 6).

The king answers that a decree written in his name and sealed with his ring cannot be revoked. But Esther and Mordecai may write another, in the king's name, as they see fit (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
A signet ring was an official's signature. Pressed into clay or wax, its seal made a document the king's own command. Giving the ring to Mordecai put the king's authority in his hands, as Pharaoh once did for Joseph.

The rule that a Persian decree could not be revoked, stated here and in the book of Daniel, meant that the king could not simply withdraw Haman's edict without undermining the authority of his own word. The way out is a second decree that answers the first.

Esther's grief is for her people, not only for herself. She has her own life back. She weeps for her kindred.
passages.later: Pharaoh gave Joseph his ring in the same way: ‘Then Pharaoh removed the signet ring from his finger, put it on Joseph’s finger’ (Genesis 41:42).
passages.asks: Esther was safe, and she still fell at the king's feet weeping for others. Ask whether you stop caring about a danger once it no longer touches you. And ask what it would mean to keep pleading for those who are still at risk.

passages.t: Mordecai's decree, and a day of light
passages.happening:
On the twenty-third day of the third month, the royal scribes write Mordecai's orders to the satraps, governors and princes of all the provinces, in every script and language (verse 9). He writes in the king's name and seals it with the king's ring, and mounted couriers carry it out on the king's horses (verse 10).

The king permits the Jews in every city to gather and defend themselves against any armed force that would attack them, on the same day Haman had set, the thirteenth of Adar (verses 11-12), and the edict is published so that ‘the Jews would be ready on that day’ (verse 13).

‘Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal garments of blue and white, with a large gold crown and a purple robe of fine linen. And the city of Susa shouted and rejoiced’ (verse 15). ‘For the Jews it was a time of light and gladness, of joy and honor’ (verse 16). And ‘many of the people of the land themselves became Jews, because the fear of the Jews had fallen upon them’ (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The new decree is dated about two months after Haman's, in about 474 BC, leaving some nine months before the thirteenth of Adar, when both decrees would take effect.

Much of this chapter repeats the words of chapter 3 on purpose. The same scribes are called, the same list of officials and provinces appears, the same ring seals the letters, and the same couriers ride out. Every instrument once used against the Jews is now used for them.

The Persian courier system was famous in the ancient world: relays of horsemen along the royal roads, each riding one stage and passing the message on.

Verse 16 piles up four words, light, gladness, joy and honor, to express the flood of relief. The verse later became part of Jewish ritual. And verse 17 ends with a surprise: many of the peoples of the land became Jews, or declared themselves on the side of the Jews. The verb is found only here in the Hebrew Bible, and whether it means conversion, taking sides, or both is debated.
passages.later: The same couriers had carried Haman's decree, as the book told in its third chapter: ‘The couriers left, spurred on by the king’s command’ (3:15). The psalmist knew the same turn from sorrow to joy: ‘You turned my mourning into dancing’ (Psalm 30:11).
passages.hard:
Does Mordecai's decree permit the killing of women and children?

Verse 11 in many translations, the BSB among them, reads as though the Jews were allowed to kill the women and children of those who attacked them, echoing the words of Haman's decree in 3:13. That reading troubles many readers.

Some Hebrew scholars argue that the phrase more naturally describes the Jews' own women and children as the ones the enemy would attack, so that the decree lets the Jews defend themselves against anyone who would assault them, their wives and their children. The grammar allows both readings, and translators differ.

Chapter 9, which tells what actually happened, counts men killed in Susa, says nothing of women or children, and stresses that the Jews took no plunder. Whatever the exact sense of the decree, the book presents it as a defensive answer to a legal order for the destruction of a people, not as a license for slaughter. Nothing in it gives anyone today a warrant to harm anyone.
passages.asks: The decree that brought fear became a decree that brought light and gladness. Ask where you have seen a harm turned to good in your own life or someone else's. And ask how you can share that joy, as the Jews of every city did.
